A stock selloff driven by doubts about the economic growth potential of artificial intelligence infected commodities, too, dragging crude oil prices down today despite continued tanker attacks in the Persian Gulf.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $92.55 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at $83.45 per barrel. Both were down from the opening of trade in Asia, but they were both higher than their Friday close, suggesting the effect of the stock selloff was limited in energy commodities.

The selloff was triggered by developments in the tech sector, with investors questioning the prospects of the AI industry, whose growth is being fuelled by tens of billions in borrowed funds, as noted by Reuters. These doubts apparently flourished last week around Anthropic’s IPO, causing a 10% drop in Nasdaq—the sharpest drop since the pandemic lockdowns.

Tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz have become a daily occurrence, based on reports from official Iranian and international sources, with incidents both in the strait itself and outside it, off the coast of Oman. Meanwhile, the Yemeni Houthis continue to strike targets in Saudi Arabia. The latest, according to the Houthis themselves, was a refinery on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast.

Meanwhile, the COP31 gathering failed to result in a deal on global emission reduction efforts as countries could not agree on whether the world should phase out oil and gas, and who will pay for it all. This is the first time the Conference of the Parties has failed to end in a deal since 2009.

Oil prices have been on a losing streak for three weeks now, largely on reports about supply catching up to demand and even exceeding it, despite the flow of incident reports from the Persian Gulf. Interestingly, not everyone agrees the glut is here, with the IEA expecting it in the current quarter, while OPEC focuses on a demand rebound.
